{{Short description|American composer}}{{More citations needed|date=May 2026}}{{for|Hiller's father, the photographer and illustrator|Lejaren Hiller Sr.}}
'''Lejaren Arthur Hiller Jr.''' (February 23, 1924 – January 26, 1994)<ref name="Gena">[http://www.petergena.com/lhobit.html Lejaren Hiller (1924–1994)] © 1994 by Peter Gena.</ref><ref name="NYTimes">Kozinn, Allan (February 1, 1994)[https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/01/obituaries/lejaren-hiller-69-first-composer-to-write-music-with-a-computer.html "Lejaren Hiller, 69, First Composer To Write Music With a Computer"], NYTimes.com; accessed July 1, 2017.</ref><ref name="Di Nunzio">{{cite web |last=Di Nunzio |first=Alex |title=Lejaren Hiller |work=MusicInformatica |url=http://www.musicainformatica.org/topics/lejaren-hiller.php |accessdate=5 September 2017 |date=1 October 2013 |publisher=MusicaInformatica}}</ref> was an American composer, computer scientist, and chemist.

==Career==
Hiller was born on February 23, 1924, in New York City. His father, [[Lejaren Hiller Sr.]], was a well-known art photographer who specialized in historical tableaux.{{citation needed|date=July 2017}} As a child, Lejaren Jr. played piano, oboe, clarinet, and saxophone. While earning a degree in chemistry at [[Princeton University]], he also studied composition with [[Roger Sessions]] and [[Milton Babbitt]].<ref name="NYTimes"/> From 1947 to 1952, he worked as a research chemist for [[DuPont]] in [[Waynesboro, Virginia]], where he developed the first reliable process for dyeing Orlon [[acrylic fiber]] and coauthored a popular textbook.<ref name="Bohn">[http://www.stonehill.edu/directory/james-bohn/ Bohn, James] (undated). [http://ems.music.illinois.edu/ems/history/hiller Lejaren Hiller"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227231835/http://ems.music.illinois.edu/ems/history/hiller |date=2017-02-27 }}, illinois.edu; accessed February 26, 2017. {{verification needed|date=February 2017|reason=The terms "text", "book", "author", and "Orlon" can not be found in the article. The NY Times says he wrote three books, this would be a fourth.}}</ref>

In 1957, he collaborated with [[Leonard Isaacson]] on his ''[[Illiac Suite]]'',<ref name="Di Nunzio"/> the first significant work of computer-based [[algorithmic composition]], which was realized using the [[ILLIAC I]] computer at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]]. He wrote an article on the ''Illiac Suite'' for ''[[Scientific American]]'' which garnered controversy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hiller |first=Lejaren A. |date=1959 |title=COMPUTER MUSIC |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24941187 |journal=Scientific American |volume=201 |issue=6 |pages=109–121 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1259-109 |jstor=24941187 |bibcode=1959SciAm.201f.109H |issn=0036-8733|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Hiller was met with hostility from the musical establishment; both ''[[Baker's Biographical Dictionary of Musicians]]'' and ''[[The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians]]'' refused to include him until shortly before his death.{{citation needed|date=January 2017}}

A majority of Hiller's works after 1957 do not involve computers at all, but might include [[stochastic music]], [[Indeterminacy (music)|indeterminacy]], [[serialism]], Brahmsian traditionalism, jazz, [[performance art]], folk song and [[counterpoint]] mixed together. In 1958, Hiller founded the [[Experimental Music Studios]] at the University of Illinois. He created the MUSICOMP ("MUsic SImulator-Interpreter for COMpositional Procedures") [[programming language]] for music composition with Robert Baker in order to create their ''Computer Cantata'' (1963).<ref name="Bohn"/><ref name="Di Nunzio"/> He also collaborated with [[John Cage]] for the composition and multimedia event ''[[HPSCHD]]'' (1969).<ref name="Gena"/><ref name="NYTimes"/>

In 1968, he joined the faculty at the [[University at Buffalo]] as Slee Professor of Composition, where he established the school's first computer music facility, co-directed with [[Lukas Foss]], at the Center of the Creative and Performing Arts. Illness forced him to retire in 1989.<ref name="Gena"/><ref name="NYTimes"/>

His notable pupils include [[James Fulkerson]], [[Larry Lake (musician)|Larry Lake]], [[Ilza Nogueira]], [[David Rosenboom]], [[Margaret Scoville]], Michael Ranta, [[Elliott Sharp]], [[Bernadette Speach]], and [[James Tenney]]. 

Hiller died from [[Alzheimer's disease]] on January 26, 1994, in [[Buffalo, New York]].<ref name="Gena"/><ref name="NYTimes"/>

==Bibliography==
Hiller wrote three books:<ref name="NYTimes"/>
*Hiller, Lejaren A., and [[Leonard Issacson|Leonard M. Issacson]]. (1959/1979). ''Experimental Music: Composition With an Electronic Computer''. McGraw-Hill, New York. {{ISBN|978-0-313-22158-3}}.
*Hiller, Lejaren and Herber, Rolfe H. (1960). ''Principles of Chemistry''.
*Hiller, Lejaren (1964). ''Informationstheorie und Computermusik''. {{in lang|de}}
